claims.source: While it is part of most animals' normal behavioral repertoire, maladaptive aggression in humans takes an enormous toll on society (Filley et al., 2001; Miczek et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claims.claim: Classical experiments in cats and rodents revealed the existence of localized 'centers' in the medial hypothalamus, whose artificial electrical stimulation was sufficient to trigger attack behavior.
claims.source: Classical experiments in cats and rodents revealed the existence of localized 'centers' in the medial hypothalamus, whose artificial electrical stimulation was sufficient to trigger attack behavior (Hess, 1928; Hess and Brügger, 1943; reviewed in Siegel et al., 1999; Kruk, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple citations to classical studies.

claims.claim: Neurons responsible for hypothalamic aggression centers were identified in the murine ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH), using steroid hormone receptors as molecular markers, and optogenetics.
claims.source: Recently, the neurons responsible for this activity were identified in the murine ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH), using steroid hormone receptors as molecular markers, and optogenetics (Lin et al., 2011; Lee et al., 2014) or genetically targeted cell ablation (Yang et al., 2013; reviewed in Falkner and Lin, 2014; Kennedy et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to recent studies.

claims.claim: VMH neurons number approximately 2,000 per hemisphere.
claims.source: Interestingly, although these cells number ~2,000 per hemisphere, they play a role in male-female mating behavior as well as in fighting (Lin et al., 2011; Sano et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claims.claim: VMH neurons play a role in male-female mating behavior as well as in fighting.
claims.source: Interestingly, although these cells number ~2,000 per hemisphere, they play a role in male-female mating behavior as well as in fighting (Lin et al., 2011; Sano et al., 2013; Yang et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple citations.

claims.claim: Drosophila melanogaster presents an attractive alternative model for dissecting the neural circuitry of aggression because of the reduced complexity of its nervous system and the availability of genetic tools.
claims.source: Drosophila melanogaster presents an attractive alternative model for dissecting the neural circuitry of aggression, because of the reduced complexity of its nervous system and the availability of genetic tools for marking and manipulating specific neuronal cell types (Baier et al., 2002; Kravitz and Huber, 2003; Zwarts et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claims.claim: Drosophila males exhibit robust aggressive behavior, which consists of different agonistic actions such as wing threat, lunging, tussling and boxing.
claims.source: Drosophila males exhibit robust aggressive behavior, which consists of different agonistic actions such as wing threat, lunging, tussling and boxing (Dow and von Schilcher, 1975; Skrzipek et al., 1979; Hoffmann, 1987; Chen et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claims.claim: Aggression in flies reflects competition over resources such as food, territory or females.
claims.source: Aggression in flies, as in other species, reflects competition over resources such as food, territory or females (Hoffmann and Cacoyianni, 1990; Chen et al., 2002; Hoyer et al., 2008; Lim et al., 2014; Yuan et al., 2014), and is under genetic control (Dierick and Greenspan, 2006; Zwarts et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claims.claim: Aggression in flies is under genetic control.
claims.source: Aggression in flies, as in other species, reflects competition over resources such as food, territory or females (Hoffmann and Cacoyianni, 1990; Chen et al., 2002; Hoyer et al., 2008; Lim et al., 2014; Yuan et al., 2014), and is under genetic control (Dierick and Greenspan, 2006; Zwarts et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claims.claim: The male-specific form of the sex-determination gene fruitless (fruM) is required for normal intermale aggression in Drosophila.
claims.source: The male-specific form of the sex-determination gene fruitless (fruM) is required for normal intermale aggression in Drosophila (Vrontou et al., 2006) and genetic feminization of relatively broad neuronal populations can feminize (Nilsen et al., 2004) aggressive behavior (Certel et al., 2007; Chan and Kravitz, 2007; Mundiyanapurath et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claims.claim: DTKFruM neurons represent the first subclass of FruM-expressing neurons that appears specific to the control of aggression.
claims.source: Thus, DTKFruM neurons represent the first subclass of FruM-expressing neurons that appears specific to the control of aggression.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction based on previous work by the authors.

claims.claim: Of the 3038 lines screened, 815 lines had phenotypes that interfered with the ability to engage in social behaviors.
claims.source: Of the 3038 lines screened (Figure 1A), 815 lines had phenotypes that interfered with the ability to engage in social behaviors.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the screen.

claims.claim: 19 GAL4 lines showed a significant increase in one or more aggressive behaviors compared to the control line.
claims.source: Of the remaining lines, 19 showed a significant increase in one or more aggressive behaviors, compared to an enhancer-less GAL4 control line BDPG4U (pBDPGAL4u; Pfeiffer et al., 2010) (Figure 1A and B), which does not drive expression in the central nervous system (CNS) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 1.

claims.claim: Three GAL4 lines exhibited both increased aggression and increased inter-male courtship measured as unilateral wing extension.
claims.source: Interestingly, three of these aggression-promoting lines, including R15A01-GAL4, R71G01-GAL4 and R22G11-GAL4, also displayed a robust increase in courtship behavior as measured by wing extension (Figure 1B, inset; Video 1).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 1B.

claims.claim: The P1a spGAL4 driver labeled approximately 8–10 FruM-expressing P1 neurons per hemibrain.
claims.source: Indeed, the spGAL4 intersection of R15A01-AD and R71G01-DBD (henceforth referred to as P1a spGAL4) labeled approximately 8–10 FruM-expressing P1 neurons per hemibrain (see also Inagaki et al., 2013); no labeling was observed in the ventral nerve cord (VNC) (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 1E.

claims.claim: The P1a spGAL4 driver labeled a minor and variable population of neurons (<4 per hemibrain) with cell bodies in the lateral horn (LH) that were neither FruM-positive nor male-specific.
claims.source: In addition to P1 neurons, the P1a spGAL4 driver labeled a minor and variable population of neurons (<4 per hemibrain) with cell bodies in the lateral horn (LH) that were neither FruM-positive nor male-specific (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: dTrpA1 activation of P1a spGAL4 males resulted in a robust, temperature-dependent increase in both aggression and wing extension.
claims.source: Strikingly, dTrpA1 activation of P1a spGAL4 males resulted in a robust, temperature-dependent increase in both aggression and wing extension (Figure 1F), compared to a control intersection of R15A01-AD and a driverless-DBD line (BDP-DBD).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 1F.

claims.claim: P1a>dTrpA1 males showed a significant increase in lunging towards wild-type target males throughout the observation period.
claims.source: In such mixed-genotype pairs, P1a>dTrpA1 males still showed a significant increase in lunging towards the WT target male throughout the observation period, in comparison to BDPG4U>dTrpA1 controls (Figures 1G, lower and 1H).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figures 1G and 1H.

claims.claim: The lunging frequency per P1a>dTrpA1 male was not significantly different between same genotype and mixed-genotype pairs.
claims.source: The lunging frequency per P1a>dTrpA1 male was not significantly different between same genotype (P1a vs P1a) and mixed-genotype pairs (P1a vs WT) (Figure 1H).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 1H.

claims.claim: Wild-type target males showed no significant lunging behavior towards the P1a>dTrpA1 aggressor.
claims.source: In contrast, the WT target males (identified by clipping the tip of one wing) showed no significant lunging behavior towards the P1a>dTrpA1 aggressor (Figure 1H, left panel, Tester: WT).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 1H.

claims.claim: The sustained increase in aggression caused by activating P1a neurons in a mixed pair does not depend on counter-attack by the target fly.
claims.source: These data indicate that the sustained increase in aggression caused by activating P1a neurons in a mixed pair does not depend on counter-attack by the target fly.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the results section based on the mixed-genotype pair experiments.

claims.claim: Increased male wing extension behavior is neither necessary nor sufficient to explain the increased aggression phenotype.
claims.source: These data indicate that increased male wing extension behavior is neither necessary nor sufficient to explain the increased aggression phenotype.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the results section based on multiple experiments.

claims.claim: The aggression phenotype reflects a fly-intrinsic influence of P1a neuron activation.
claims.source: Taken together, these results indicate that the aggression phenotype reflects a fly-intrinsic influence of P1a neuron activation.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the results section based on multiple experiments.

claims.claim: All intersectional flies with FruM+ P1 neurons exhibited a significant increase in lunging upon dTrpA1 activation.
claims.source: Despite the small number of P1 neurons labeled, all of these intersectional flies exhibited a significant increase in lunging upon dTrpA1 activation (Figures 2E and F).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figures 2E and F.

claims.claim: There was little to no enhancement of wing extension in FruM+ P1 neuron intersectional flies.
claims.source: In contrast to the enhanced aggression, however, there was little to no enhancement of wing extension (Figures 2E and G), consistent with earlier reports that at least 10 P1 neurons must express dTrpA1myc to significantly increase singing relative to controls (von Philipsborn et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figures 2E and G and citation to von Philipsborn et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Activation of just a few FruM P1 neurons is sufficient to increase aggression.
claims.source: These observations indicate that activation of just a few FruM P1 neurons is sufficient to increase aggression.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the results section based on the FruM+ P1 neuron experiments.

claims.claim: Increased aggression can be observed in the absence of elevated wing extension.
claims.source: They also demonstrate that the increased aggression phenotype can be observed in the absence of elevated wing extension, further dissociating these two behavioral phenotypes of P1 neuron activation.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the results section based on the FruM+ P1 neuron experiments.

claims.claim: A linear increase in the magnitude of GCaMP6s responses from each P1 neuron was observed as the photostimulation frequency was increased from 10 to 50 Hz.
claims.source: We observed a linear increase in the magnitude of GCaMP6s responses from each P1 neuron as the PS frequency was increased from 10 to 50 Hz.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: As the photostimulation frequency was increased from 1 to 20 Hz, there was a progressive increase in lunging rate by P1a>CsChrimson vs. BDPG4U>CsChrimson control flies.
claims.source: In freely behaving male fly pairs, as the PS frequency was increased from 1 to 20 Hz, there was a progressive increase in lunging rate by P1a>CsChrimson vs. BDPG4U>CsChrimson control flies (Figures 3A and B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figures 3A and B.

claims.claim: At 10 Hz and above, the lunging rate was significantly higher than that of genetic controls stimulated at the same frequency.
claims.source: At 10 Hz and above (the threshold frequency that yielded a significant increase in GCaMP6 responses; Figure 3—figure supplement 1) the lunging rate was significantly higher than that of genetic controls stimulated at the same frequency (Figure 3C, blue vs. white bars), and of pre-stimulation baseline lunging levels in the experimental genotype (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: The enhancement of aggression in P1a>CsChrimson flies was not time-locked to the onset of photostimulation, but rather tended to increase following photostimulation offset.
claims.source: However, the enhancement of aggression in P1a>CsChrimson flies was not time-locked to the onset of PS, but rather tended to increase following PS offset (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: Across the photostimulation frequency range of 1–20 Hz, there was little promotion of wing extension.
claims.source: Importantly, across this same frequency range (1–20 Hz) there was little promotion of wing extension (Figures 3A and D, red lines/bars; Figure 3F, red lines).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figures 3A, D, and F.

claims.claim: The threshold for optogenetic enhancement of aggression by P1a neurons is lower than that required for wing extension.
claims.source: These data indicate that the threshold for optogenetic enhancement of aggression by P1a neurons is lower than that required for wing extension, under these conditions.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the results section based on the optogenetic experiments.

claims.claim: Aggression was increasingly suppressed during the light ON phase as the photostimulation frequency was raised above the threshold for evoking wing extension.
claims.source: As the PS frequency was raised above the threshold for evoking wing extension, we observed that aggression was increasingly suppressed during the light ON phase (Figure 3C, 30–50 Hz, shaded regions; Figure 3G, 'ON'; Video 4).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 3C and 3G.

claims.claim: Following photostimulation offset, aggression rapidly resumed and wing extension was concomitantly suppressed.
claims.source: Following PS offset, however, aggression rapidly resumed and wing extension was concomitantly suppressed (Figures 3A and C, 30–50 Hz, blue bars; Figure 3G; see also Figure 3—figure supplement 2E for 50 Hz PS; Video 4).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figures 3A, C, and G.

claims.claim: High-frequency P1 activation promoted extended periods of locomotor arrest, which was relieved following photostimulation offset.
claims.source: We also observed that high-frequency P1 activation promoted extended periods of locomotor arrest, which was relieved following PS offset (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C-E).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 2C-E.

claims.claim: A relatively rapid decline of wing extension was observed following the offset of high-frequency photostimulation.
claims.source: Conversely, we observed a relatively rapid decline of wing extension following the offset of high-frequency PS (Figures 3A and D, red; 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 2E; t1/2 = 9 ± 3 s), concomitant with the re-initiation of aggression.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figures 3A, D, and G.

claims.claim: Silencing of TKFruM neurons strongly suppressed the enhancement of lunging that occurred following termination of P1 photoactivation.
claims.source: Indeed, silencing of TKFruM neurons using Kir2.1 (Baines et al., 2001) strongly suppressed the enhancement of lunging that occurred following termination of P1 photoactivation (Figure 3H, lunging, blue box and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A, bottom raster).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claims.claim: TKFruM neurons are either functionally downstream of P1 neurons, or act in a parallel pathway required for aggression.
claims.source: This result indicates that TKFruM neurons are either functionally downstream of P1 neurons, or act in a parallel pathway required for aggression.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the results section based on the epistasis experiment.

claims.claim: Silencing TKFruM neurons caused a strong and statistically significant increase in wing extension during the light OFF period.
claims.source: Strikingly, although silencing TKFruM neurons had no effect to diminish or enhance wing extension during PS (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and B), it caused a strong and statistically significant increase in wing extension during the light OFF period (Figure 3H, right, red box; Figure 3—figure supplement 3A, bottom raster).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claims.claim: Silencing of TKFruM neurons in male pairs allowed P1a activation-induced wing extension to persist into the post-stimulation period, similar to the response of solitary flies.
claims.source: In other words, silencing of TKFruM neurons in male pairs allowed P1a activation-induced wing extension to persist into the post-stimulation period, similar to the response of solitary flies (Inagaki et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Inagaki et al., 2013.

claims.claim: The rapid decrease in wing extension observed following the offset of photostimulation is caused by the resumption of aggression.
claims.source: These data indicate that the rapid decrease in wing extension observed following the offset of photostimulation (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 2E) is indeed caused by the resumption of aggression.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the results section based on the epistasis experiment.

claims.claim: A significant reduction in the frequency of lunging following transient P1a photoactivation was observed when P1a>ReaChR males were paired with target males lacking oenocytes.
claims.source: Under these conditions, a significant reduction in the frequency of lunging following transient P1a photoactivation was observed, in comparison to P1a>ReaChR males paired with control male targets bearing intact oenocytes (oe+) (Figure 3I).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 3I.

claims.claim: The abrupt switch from enhanced wing extension to enhanced fighting following the offset of P1a activation requires appropriate chemosensory cues on the conspecific target.
claims.source: Thus, the abrupt switch from enhanced wing extension to enhanced fighting following the offset of P1a activation requires appropriate chemosensory cues on the conspecific target.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the results section based on the oenocyte ablation experiment.

claims.claim: Ongoing aggression was observed in the 1 min intervals between successive episodes of high-frequency P1a neuron activation.
claims.source: The fact that ongoing aggression was observed in the 1 min intervals between successive episodes of high-frequency P1a neuron activation (Figure 3A) indicated that this behavior, once triggered, could be sustained at least briefly without continued PS.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Wing extension was robustly induced during photostimulation but switched to aggression following photostimulation offset in P1a>ReaChR male pairs exposed to one 1-min episode of photoactivation.
claims.source: Under these conditions, wing extension was robustly induced during PS, but switched to aggression following PS offset; this lunging persisted for at least 10 min (Figures 4A−C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figures 4A-C.

claims.claim: Robust, persistent aggression could be triggered by weaker photostimulation conditions that promoted only occasional wing extension bouts in a subset of flies.
claims.source: Such robust, persistent aggression could also be triggered by weaker photosimulation conditions that promoted only occasional wing extension bouts in a subset of flies (Figures 4D−F).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figures 4D-F.

claims.claim: Persistent post-photostimulation aggression was triggered even in the cohort of fly pairs that showed no wing extension at all during the photostimulation period.
claims.source: Under these latter conditions, persistent post-PS aggression was triggered even in the cohort of fly pairs (8/22) that showed no wing extension at all during the PS period (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Persistent aggression could be promoted by a single episode of P1a neuronal activation, and did not depend on male-male wing extension behavior during photostimulation.
claims.source: Thus, persistent aggression could be promoted by a single episode of P1a neuronal activation, and did not depend on male-male wing extension behavior during PS.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the results section based on the experiments in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Persistent attack towards a wild-type target lasting at least 10 min was triggered by a single episode of photostimulation when P1a>ReaChR flies were paired with a group-housed, non-aggressive wild-type target fly.
claims.source: Under these conditions, persistent attack towards the WT target lasting at least 10 min was triggered by a single episode of photostimulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B.

claims.claim: Persistent aggression was not simply perpetuated by self-sustaining cycles of attack and counter-attack, but likely reflected a long-lived internal state in the tester fly.
claims.source: These results suggested that persistent aggression was not simply perpetuated by self-sustaining cycles of attack and counter-attack, but likely reflected a long-lived internal state in the tester fly.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the results section based on the mixed-genotype pair experiments.

claims.claim: Separated P1a>ReaChR males showed a robust increase in wing extension during photostimulation, which persisted after light offset.
claims.source: As expected, separated P1a>ReaChR males (Figure 5B), but not BDPG4U>ReaChR males (Figure 5C), showed a robust increase in wing extension during PS, which persisted after light offset (Inagaki et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figures 5B and C and citation to Inagaki et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Upon removal of the barrier 1 min after photostimulation offset, P1a>ReaChR males switched to aggression.
claims.source: Upon removal of the barrier 1 min after PS offset (a time when the flies were still performing wing extensions), these P1a >ReaChR males switched to aggression (Figures 5B, blue rasters).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Enhanced aggression was observed even when removal of the barrier was delayed for 10 min after the offset of photostimulation.
claims.source: Strikingly, enhanced aggression was observed even when removal of the barrier was delayed for 10 min after the offset of PS (Figures 5D and E) (Video 5), by which time persistent wing extension behavior (Figure 5F), as well as locomotor activity (see Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), had decayed to baseline levels for at least 5 min.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figures 5D, E, and F.

claims.claim: The level of lunging after barrier removal for both the 1 min and 10 min conditions was significantly elevated compared to BDPG4U>ReaChR controls.
claims.source: The level of lunging after barrier removal for both the 1 min and 10 min conditions was significantly elevated compared to BDPG4U>ReaChR controls (Figure 5G), as well as control P1a>ReaChR males that received no PS (Figure 5H).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figures 5G and H.

claims.claim: The latency to lunging was not significantly different between barrier removal at 1 min vs. 10 min.
claims.source: Although the latency to lunging was not significantly different between barrier removal at 1 min vs. 10 min (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D), the flies took longer to achieve maximal levels of aggression in the latter case, suggestive of a decay in the internal state promoted by P1a activation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: P1 neuron activation triggers a persistent internal state facilitating future social behaviors, which can endure for minutes in behaviorally quiescent solitary flies.
claims.source: Together, these experiments suggest that P1 neuron activation triggers a persistent internal state facilitating future social behaviors, which can endure for minutes in behaviorally quiescent solitary flies.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the results section based on the barrier experiments.

claims.claim: The identification of P1 neurons in a screen for aggression-promoting neurons was surprising, as the prevailing view is that these cells specifically promote male courtship behavior.
claims.source: The identification of P1 neurons in a screen for aggression-promoting neurons was surprising, as the prevailing view is that these cells specifically promote male courtship behavior, in response to female-specific pheromones (Kohatsu et al., 2011; von Philipsborn et al., 2011; Pan et al., 2012; Clowney et al., 2015; Kallman et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations.

claims.claim: Activation of P1 neurons promotes aggression in a fly-intrinsic manner, and is not an indirect social response provoked by elevated wing extension behavior.
claims.source: These data suggest that activation of P1 neurons promotes aggression in a fly-intrinsic manner, and is not an indirect social response provoked by elevated wing extension behavior.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the discussion based on the experimental results.

claims.claim: Attempts to demonstrate a requirement for P1 neurons during spontaneous aggression using various methods of cell inactivation or ablation have been unsuccessful.
claims.source: Unfortunately, attempts to demonstrate a requirement for P1 neurons during spontaneous aggression using various methods of cell inactivation or ablation have so far been unsuccessful.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion.

claims.claim: While artificial activation of P1 neurons can promote aggression, it remains unclear whether they are normally required for this behavior.
claims.source: Thus, while artificial activation of P1 neurons can promote aggression, it remains unclear whether they are normally required for this behavior, and if so under what circumstances.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a caveat in the discussion.

claims.claim: The effect of P1 neurons to promote aggression vs. wing extension could be uncoupled by systematically manipulating the level of activation using red-shifted optogenetic effectors.
claims.source: We found that the effect of P1 neurons to promote aggression vs. wing extension could be uncoupled, by systematically manipulating the level of activation using red-shifted optogenetic effectors.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion summarizing the optogenetic experiments.

claims.claim: At low frequencies of photostimulation (≤20 Hz), a modest but significant increase in aggression was evoked, without any accompanying increase in unilateral wing extension behavior.
claims.source: At low frequencies of photostimulation (≤20 Hz), a modest but significant increase in aggression was evoked, without any accompanying increase in unilateral wing extension behavior.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion summarizing the optogenetic experiments.

claims.claim: Wing extension was evoked at photostimulation frequencies above 30 Hz.
claims.source: Wing extension was evoked at photostimulation frequencies above 30 Hz.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion summarizing the optogenetic experiments.

claims.claim: Output from the P1 population can control different behaviors at different thresholds.
claims.source: These data suggest that output from the P1 population can control different behaviors at different thresholds.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the discussion based on the optogenetic experiments.

claims.claim: Studies of hypothalamic circuits in mice have revealed a threshold-dependent influence of optogenetic activation on mating and aggression.
claims.source: Nevertheless, it is of interest that studies of hypothalamic circuits in mice have also revealed a threshold-dependent influence of optogenetic activation on mating and aggression (although opposite to the direction observed here) (Hong et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations.

claims.claim: At high stimulation frequencies (≥30 Hz), wing extension was promoted during the light ON phase, while aggression was suppressed.
claims.source: The temporal resolution afforded by optogenetic activation of P1 neurons also revealed an inverse relationship between the promotion of these two behaviors: at high stimulation frequencies (≥30 Hz), wing extension was promoted during the light ON phase, while aggression was suppressed; conversely, during the light OFF phase, aggression resumed and wing extension was suppressed.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion summarizing the optogenetic experiments.

claims.claim: During the light OFF phase, aggression resumed and wing extension was suppressed.
claims.source: The temporal resolution afforded by optogenetic activation of P1 neurons also revealed an inverse relationship between the promotion of these two behaviors: at high stimulation frequencies (≥30 Hz), wing extension was promoted during the light ON phase, while aggression was suppressed; conversely, during the light OFF phase, aggression resumed and wing extension was suppressed.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion summarizing the optogenetic experiments.

claims.claim: When aggression is inhibited by silencing TK-GAL41 neurons, wing extension triggered by optogenetic activation of P1a neurons persists into the light OFF phase.
claims.source: Our cellular epistasis experiment revealed that when aggression is inhibited, by silencing TK-GAL41 neurons (Asahina et al., 2014), wing extension triggered by optogenetic activation of P1a neurons persists into the light OFF phase, as described previously for single male flies (Inagaki et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to Asahina et al., 2014 and Inagaki et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Aggressive behavior causally suppresses wing extension following the offset of photostimulation.
claims.source: This result indicates that aggressive behavior causally suppresses wing extension following the offset of photostimulation, suggestive of an inhibitory influence at the neural circuit or behavioral level.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the discussion based on the epistasis experiment.

claims.claim: The suppression of lunging during the light ON phase may reflect a reciprocal inhibitory influence of courtship circuitry on aggression.
claims.source: By extension, the suppression of lunging during the light ON phase may reflect a reciprocal inhibitory influence of courtship circuitry on aggression (however, the acute suppression of locomotor activity produced by strong optogenetic activation of P1 neurons may contribute to the inhibition of aggression as well).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a speculation in the discussion.

claims.claim: Reciprocal inhibitory influences between circuits controlling 'opponent' behaviors is well established.
claims.source: The existence of reciprocal inhibitory influences between circuits controlling 'opponent' behaviors is well established (reviewed in Kristan, 2008).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to Kristan, 2008.

claims.claim: Transient activation of P1 neurons triggers persistent wing extension in solitary males.
claims.source: Previously, it was shown that transient activation of P1 neurons triggers persistent wing extension in solitary males (Inagaki et al., 2013; Bath et al., 2014; Clowney et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations.

claims.claim: Transient activation of P1 neurons can result in enhanced aggression, even when physical contact between the flies was delayed for 10 min.
claims.source: This experiment revealed that transient activation of P1 neurons could result in enhanced aggression, even when physical contact between the flies was delayed for 10 min, long after persistent singing had decayed to baseline.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion summarizing the barrier experiments.

claims.claim: Activation of P1 neurons can induce a persistent, fly-intrinsic internal state that facilitates future social behavior.
claims.source: Thus, activation of P1 neurons can induce a persistent, fly-intrinsic internal state (e.g., of arousal or motivation) that facilitates future social behavior.

results.result: A large-scale thermogenetic screen of 3038 GAL4 lines identified 19 hits with increased aggression, of which 3 lines also showed increased inter-male courtship (wing extension). The screen demonstrated high specificity with only ~0.6% of lines showing aggression phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C22-C24, C102-C103 collectively describe the screen methodology and outcomes with consistent numbers across claims. The screen design, sample size (3038 lines), hit rate (19 aggression hits, 3 with dual phenotypes), and specificity are well-documented in Figure 1A-B and the text. The automated scoring system (CADABRA) and statistical validation against controls provide robust support.

results.result: Split-GAL4 intersectional genetics revealed that 8-10 FruM+ P1 interneurons per hemibrain, previously thought to control only courtship, are sufficient to promote both aggression and wing extension. P1 neurons were independently identified in three separate screen hits.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C25-C27, C104-C105 describe the genetic intersection strategy and identification of P1 neurons. The split-GAL4 data (Figure 1E-F) clearly show labeling of 8-10 P1 neurons, and behavioral assays demonstrate both aggression and courtship phenotypes. The independent recovery in three hits (0.1% of screened lines) and successful isolation through intersectional combinations strongly support the specificity and reproducibility of the finding.

results.result: P1a neuron activation promotes aggression in a fly-intrinsic manner that does not depend on counter-attack or elevated wing extension behavior. Mixed-genotype experiments showed P1a>dTrpA1 males lunged at non-aggressive wild-type targets without reciprocal aggression.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C33 describe mixed-genotype pair experiments (Figure 1G-H) demonstrating that P1a activation causes sustained aggression toward non-aggressive targets. The data show no significant difference in lunging between same-genotype and mixed-genotype pairs, while WT targets showed no lunging. This effectively rules out social feedback mechanisms and demonstrates fly-intrinsic effects. The controls (wingless flies, other GAL4 lines) further support dissociation from wing extension.

results.result: Activation of just a few (1-7) FruM+ P1 neurons is sufficient to increase aggression without enhancing wing extension, demonstrating that these behaviors can be dissociated and that aggression requires fewer activated P1 neurons than courtship.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C37 describe FruFLP intersection experiments (Figure 2) showing that small numbers of P1 neurons (1-7 per hemibrain) produce significant aggression without wing extension. This is consistent with prior work (von Philipsborn et al., 2011) showing ≥10 P1 neurons are needed for singing. The data clearly demonstrate behavioral dissociation and different thresholds, though the FruFLP system's inefficiency is acknowledged.

results.result: Optogenetic experiments revealed that P1 neurons promote aggression and wing extension at different activation thresholds. Low-frequency stimulation (≤20 Hz) enhanced aggression without wing extension, while high-frequency stimulation (≥30 Hz) evoked wing extension. Calcium imaging confirmed linear increases in P1 activity across 10-50 Hz stimulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C38-C42, C44, C73-C76 describe systematic optogenetic frequency titration experiments (Figure 3A-D, F). The calcium imaging data (Figure 3—supplement 1) validate that stimulation frequencies correlate with P1 activity levels. The behavioral data clearly show threshold-dependent effects with statistical comparisons to controls. However, the authors appropriately caution that these thresholds may reflect artificial stimulation conditions rather than natural behavior.

results.result: High-frequency P1 activation (≥30 Hz) promoted wing extension and suppressed aggression during photostimulation, while aggression rapidly resumed and wing extension was suppressed following stimulation offset. High-frequency activation also caused locomotor arrest during stimulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C6, C45-C48, C78-C79 describe the inverse temporal relationship between aggression and courtship at high stimulation frequencies (Figure 3A, C, D, G). The data show clear suppression of aggression during light ON and rapid resumption after light OFF, with concomitant changes in wing extension. The locomotor arrest observation (Figure 3—supplement 2C-E) provides a potential mechanistic explanation for aggression suppression during stimulation.

results.result: Epistasis experiments showed that silencing TKFruM neurons suppressed post-stimulation aggression but allowed wing extension to persist after P1 activation, indicating that aggressive behavior causally suppresses wing extension and that TKFruM neurons are downstream or parallel to P1 in aggression circuits.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C53, C80-C81 describe genetic epistasis experiments (Figure 3H, Figure 3—supplement 3) using Kir2.1 to silence TKFruM neurons. The results clearly show that blocking aggression allows wing extension to persist post-stimulation, similar to solitary flies. This provides strong evidence for causal suppression of courtship by aggression circuitry. The interpretation that TKFruM neurons are downstream/parallel is appropriately cautious.

results.result: The switch from wing extension to aggression following P1 activation offset requires male-specific chemosensory cues, as demonstrated by reduced post-stimulation aggression when P1a>ReaChR males were paired with oenocyte-ablated targets lacking cuticular hydrocarbons.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C55 describe oenocyte ablation experiments (Figure 3I) showing that removal of pheromone-producing cells significantly reduces post-stimulation aggression. This demonstrates sensory dependence for the behavioral switch. The experiment is well-controlled with oe+ vs oe- comparisons, though the mechanism (whether P1 neurons themselves require these cues or downstream circuits do) remains unclear.

results.result: A single episode of P1 neuron activation triggered persistent aggression lasting at least 10 minutes, which did not require wing extension behavior during photostimulation. Even flies showing no wing extension during stimulation exhibited persistent post-stimulation aggression.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C60 describe single-pulse optogenetic experiments (Figure 4) demonstrating persistent aggression after brief P1 activation. The data show aggression persisting 10+ minutes after stimulation under both strong (Figure 4A-C) and weak (Figure 4D-F) conditions. Critically, Figure 4—supplement 1 shows that flies with no wing extension during stimulation still exhibited persistent aggression, definitively dissociating the two behaviors.

results.result: P1 activation triggers a persistent internal state that can endure for at least 10 minutes in behaviorally quiescent solitary flies. Barrier experiments showed that flies photostimulated while separated still exhibited enhanced aggression when allowed to interact 10 minutes later, long after wing extension and locomotor activity returned to baseline.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C61-C68, C85-C87 describe barrier experiments (Figure 5) demonstrating a latent internal state. The experimental design elegantly separates P1 activation from social interaction. The key finding that aggression is enhanced even with 10-minute delays (Figure 5D-E), after wing extension and locomotion have returned to baseline (Figure 5F, Figure 5—supplement 1C), strongly supports a persistent internal state distinct from ongoing behavior. The state does not require generalized arousal (no locomotor increase).

results.result: P1 neurons promote a latent internal state that facilitates both aggression and courtship, while controlling their overt expression in a threshold-dependent, inverse manner. This represents a common circuit node for controlling multiple social behaviors, consistent with hierarchical models of behavioral organization.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C8, C70, C97, C99 represent the main conclusions synthesizing multiple experimental findings. The threshold-dependent control is supported by optogenetic titration (C3, C38-C44), the inverse relationship by temporal dynamics (C5-C6, C45-C46), the persistent state by barrier experiments (C4, C61-C68), and the common node concept by the dual phenotypes (C1, C24). The integration of these findings into a coherent model is well-supported, though the authors appropriately note caveats about artificial stimulation conditions.

results.result: Loss-of-function experiments using cell inactivation or ablation have not successfully demonstrated a requirement for P1 neurons in spontaneous aggression, leaving unclear whether P1 neurons are normally required for this behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C72 acknowledge negative results from loss-of-function experiments. This is an important caveat appropriately discussed by the authors. The claims are supported by the text stating these experiments were attempted but unsuccessful. The authors provide reasonable explanations (incomplete penetrance, subset expression, redundant circuits, context-dependence) but correctly conclude that the requirement for P1 in natural aggression remains uncertain.

results.result: P1 neurons themselves do not show long-lasting persistent activity after activation (measured by calcium imaging), and optogenetic activation never triggered aggression in a stimulus-locked manner during light ON, with aggression typically increasing after stimulation offset.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C89 describe observations about P1 activity patterns and behavioral timing. The calcium imaging data (Figure 3—supplement 1, cited Inagaki et al., 2013) show no persistent P1 activity. The behavioral data (Figure 3) consistently show aggression increases post-stimulation rather than during stimulation. These observations constrain mechanistic models and suggest the persistent state is implemented downstream of P1 neurons.

results.result: The discovery of P1 neurons controlling both mating and fighting in Drosophila parallels findings in mouse hypothalamus where a small population of VMH neurons controls both behaviors, suggesting this may represent an evolutionarily conserved circuit motif for organizing social behaviors.
results.evaluation: Claims C69, C100-C101 discuss evolutionary conservation and comparative neurobiology. The parallel with mouse VMH neurons is well-supported by multiple citations (Lin et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2014). The suggestion of a conserved circuit motif is appropriately presented as a hypothesis rather than proven fact. The comparison is scientifically reasonable given the functional similarities, though direct homology cannot be established.

results.result: Background claims about aggression biology, Drosophila as a model system, prior work on aggression circuits in mammals and flies, and theoretical frameworks (Tinbergen's hierarchical model) provide context for the current study.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C21, C83, C90-C91, C95-C96, C98 are background/contextual claims from the Introduction and Discussion, supported by appropriate citations. These establish the scientific context and rationale for the study. The claims accurately represent prior work and established knowledge in the field, as evidenced by the citations provided.

results.result: Speculative claims about functional implications: threshold-dependent control of mating/aggression also occurs in mice (opposite direction); P1's persistent state may represent memory of a mating partner; acute P1 activation may suppress aggression toward females during courtship; P1 may exert both inhibitory and facilitatory influences on different timescales.
results.evaluation: Claims C77, C84, C92-C94 are explicitly speculative interpretations discussed by the authors. C77 notes an interesting parallel with mice but acknowledges opposite directionality. C92-C94 propose functional hypotheses about the adaptive significance of P1's dual roles, but these are not directly tested. The speculation is reasonable and appropriately qualified, but lacks direct experimental support in this study.

results.result: The suppression of lunging during high-frequency P1 activation may reflect reciprocal inhibitory influence of courtship circuitry on aggression, though locomotor arrest may also contribute.
results.evaluation: Claim C82 proposes a mechanism for aggression suppression during high-frequency stimulation but is explicitly presented as speculation with an important caveat about locomotor arrest. While reciprocal inhibition between opponent behaviors is well-established (C83), the specific mechanism here is not definitively tested. The epistasis experiment (C49-C53) supports reciprocal inhibition in the opposite direction (aggression suppressing courtship), but the reverse is not directly demonstrated.
